newsitem.title: USA: Alleged Mexican kingpin says was drugged by police.
newsitem.headline: Alleged Mexican kingpin says was drugged by police.

text.p: Alleged drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego said on Monday he was drugged by Mexican agents in January before being flown to Houston to face cocaine trafficking and money laundering charges.

Abrego, considered at one time the most notorious cocaine smuggler in Mexico, said one of the last things he remembers following his arrest was being thrown to the floor by police agents in Mexico City after asking to meet with an attorney and requesting a court hearing to block his extradition.

"I was thrown down, they put me face down and they tied me with a rope and I felt two stings of an injection," Abrego said through a translator of his alleged drugging in offices of Mexico's federal police force.

The testimony came during the second day of hearings into whether statements Abrego made to agents of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation about his involvement in drug smuggling would be admitted as evidence during a trial scheduled to begin next week.

Abrego, who was on the FBI's 10-most-wanted list when he was captured in Mexico's northern city of Monterrey, faces up to life in prison if convicted of the drug trafficking, money laundering and bribery charges contained in a 28-count federal indictment.

As head of the "Gulf Cartel" drug-smuggling operation, Abrego was allegedly responsible for shipping up to a third of the cocaine consumed in the United States while amassing a fortune estimated at $15 billion, prosecutors said.

FBI agents said last Tuesday that Abrego admitted he was involved in international drug trafficking during an hour-long meeting with FBI and U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agents after he first arrived in Houston in January.

The agents said Abrego told them he was not responsible for the massive shipments alleged to have been smuggled into the United States by the Gulf Cartel, but hinted he could name the traffickers who were, the FBI agents said.

Abrego, testifying for the first time in the U.S. criminal proceedings on Monday, said he had only vague recollections of meeting with the federal agents and did not recall signing a document spelling out his rights under U.S. law because of the heavy dose of sedatives he was given in Mexico.

Prosecutors concede Abrego was injected with ten times the normal dose of the sedative Valium and given a heavy dose of Tafil, or Xanax, along with medication for high blood pressure before he was put onto a plane and flown to the United States.

An FBI cardiologist said Abrego appeared lucid when he was examined in Houston, but medical experts hired by his defence team said he would have been clearly impaired by the sedatives and two or three shots of Tequila he was given on the plane.
"The man was definitely under the influence of drugs," said Ernest Lykissa, a Baylor College of Medicine pharmacologist. "We're talking some very high doses here."
